interactions.label: On a peripheral blood smear from a malaria patient, only ring-stage trophozoites

params.question: On a peripheral blood smear from a malaria patient, only ring-stage trophozoites and banana-shaped gametocytes are seen — no schizonts or mature trophozoites. Which property of the infecting species explains the absence of mature stages?

answers.text: The species preferentially infects reticulocytes, which are destroyed before schizonts can mature

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Reticulocyte preference is a feature of P. vivax and P. ovale, not P. falciparum. Falciparum infects red blood cells of all ages, which is one reason it drives high parasitaemia.

answers.text: Infected red blood cells sequester in deep capillaries, removing mature stages from the peripheral circulation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. P. falciparum-infected cells adhere to the walls of deep blood vessels through sequestration, so mature trophozoites and schizonts never appear in the peripheral smear — only rings and the distinctive banana-shaped gametocytes circulate.

answers.text: Giemsa stain does not bind to falciparum schizonts, making them invisible on the smear

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Giemsa stain binds equally to all Plasmodium stages. The absence of schizonts from the peripheral smear is due to sequestration in deep vasculature, not a staining limitation.

answers.text: Banana-shaped gametocytes inhibit schizont development within the same host

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Gametocytes are sexual forms that develop independently of schizonts. The absence of schizonts in peripheral blood is because infected cells with mature stages adhere to deep vessel walls through sequestration.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the smear features of P. falciparum: only rings and banana-shaped gametocytes circulate because infected cells with mature stages adhere to deep vessel walls through sequestration.
Well done. Sequestration is the hallmark of P. falciparum pathobiology — it keeps mature stages out of the smear and drives severe complications like cerebral malaria.

interactions.label: Which stage in the Plasmodium life cycle is responsible for relapses occurring m

params.question: Which stage in the Plasmodium life cycle is responsible for relapses occurring months or years after the initial P. vivax or P. ovale infection?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Merozoites rapidly invade red blood cells after schizont rupture and do not persist dormant in the circulation.

answers.text: Sporozoites remaining in the mosquito salivary glands

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Sporozoites in the salivary glands belong to the mosquito stage. Once injected into the human host, they travel to the liver — a distinct dormant hepatic form is responsible for relapse.

Correct. In P. vivax and P. ovale, some sporozoites that enter hepatocytes become hypnozoites — dormant forms that can reactivate months or years later, restarting the erythrocytic cycle and causing clinical relapse.
Incorrect. Gametocytes are the sexual forms taken up by mosquitoes during a blood meal. They do not persist in the spleen and play no role in relapse.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: in P. vivax and P. ovale, some sporozoites become hypnozoites in the liver. These dormant forms reactivate later, causing relapse — and they are the reason primaquine is needed for radical cure.
Exactly right. Hypnozoites are unique to P. vivax and P. ovale — this is why radical cure with primaquine, the only drug that targets this dormant liver stage, is essential to prevent relapse.

interactions.label: A patient with G6PD deficiency diagnosed with Plasmodium vivax malaria cannot re

params.question: A patient with G6PD deficiency diagnosed with Plasmodium vivax malaria cannot receive any antimalarial treatment.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: The statement is false. G6PD deficiency blocks only the standard radical cure with primaquine, not all antimalarial treatment. Chloroquine treats the acute attack as usual. The radical cure is modified — weekly low-dose primaquine under supervision or an alternative agent where available.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — the statement is false. G6PD deficiency contraindicates standard-dose primaquine for radical cure because it causes haemolytic anaemia. However, the acute vivax attack is still treated with chloroquine as usual. The radical cure component is modified to weekly low-dose primaquine under close supervision, not withheld entirely.

interactions.label: Which characteristic of Leishmania donovani's life cycle explains why bone marro

params.question: Which characteristic of Leishmania donovani's life cycle explains why bone marrow or splenic aspirate — rather than a peripheral blood smear — is needed for diagnosis of kala-azar?

answers.text: Amastigotes reside within macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system, not in circulating blood cells

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. L. donovani parasitises macrophages in the spleen, liver, and bone marrow as intracellular amastigotes (Leishman-Donovan bodies). Since the parasite lives within tissue macrophages rather than circulating cells, tissue aspirates are required for microscopic identification.

answers.text: Promastigotes in the blood are too fragile to survive Giemsa staining

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Promastigotes are the flagellated form found in the sandfly gut, not in human blood. The human host harbours only amastigotes, and these reside within tissue macrophages, not in circulating blood.

answers.text: The sandfly injects parasites directly into the bone marrow during a bite

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The sandfly injects promastigotes into the skin during a blood meal. Macrophages then phagocytose them, and the parasites spread through the reticuloendothelial system to the spleen, liver, and bone marrow.

answers.text: Leishmania organisms exhibit nocturnal periodicity and are absent from daytime blood samples

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Nocturnal periodicity is a feature of Wuchereria bancrofti microfilariae, not Leishmania. L. donovani resides within tissue macrophages at all times, which is why tissue aspirates — not timed blood draws — are the diagnostic approach.

overallFeedback.feedback: Remember: L. donovani lives as amastigotes inside macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system. It is not found in circulating blood cells, so peripheral blood smears cannot detect it — bone marrow or splenic aspirates are essential for diagnosis.

Well done. Understanding where each parasite resides in the human host is key to choosing the correct diagnostic specimen — tissue aspirates for Leishmania, timed nocturnal peripheral blood for filariasis, and standard blood smears for malaria.
